Let’s dive into Chapter 3: Introducing Mindful Breathing and Emotional Calm.
Now that kids have started exploring playful movement and tuning into their bodies, it’s the perfect time to unlock the magic of mindful breathing.
Mindful breathing—it sounds simple, right? But it’s actually a powerful way for children to discover more calm, focus, and balance. By learning how to pay attention to their breath, kids start to feel like they have a little more control over what’s going on inside, even when the outside world gets a bit wild.
Think about it: breath is always there. It’s the perfect anchor for mindfulness. For little ones, it all starts with just noticing how they breathe—maybe feeling their chest or belly move, or sensing the air as it comes in and goes out. Grown-ups can help by inviting children to put a hand on their belly or chest and feel that gentle rise and fall with each breath.
Want to make it more fun? Try turning breathing into a playful adventure. Here are a few ideas:
Imagine pretending to blow up a huge, colorful balloon. Take a deep breath in, then slowly breathe out, as if you’re filling that balloon with air.
Or picture your favorite flower. Breathe in its sweet scent, then blow out gently, as if sending away a dandelion seed.
You can even grab a soft toy and rest it on your belly—watch it move up and down as you breathe. These playful tricks help kids connect with their breath in a way that’s easy to feel and see.
The goal isn’t to force deep or slow breaths. Instead, it’s about encouraging gentle curiosity—just noticing, exploring, and having fun with it.
Mindful breathing is especially helpful when big feelings show up. If a child feels upset, anxious, or totally overwhelmed, returning attention to the breath can help them feel safe and grounded again. Adults can model this, too—just take a few slow breaths, and invite the child to join whenever they feel ready.
Here are a few simple breathing techniques that can bring a little more calm:
Try counting your breaths. Inhale for a count of three, then exhale for a count of three.
Or add some movement—raise your arms overhead as you breathe in, and lower them as you breathe out.
And don’t forget the pause: notice the stillness at the top of the inhale, and again at the bottom of the exhale.
The best part? You can weave these practices into everyday moments—maybe before meals, at bedtime, or whenever you need a little extra calm.
Over time, children discover that their breath is a tool they can rely on. It helps them handle the ups and downs of growing up, and gives them a way to find calm, no matter what life brings.
